one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detectors are effectively closed-vocabulary: novel-class success is concentrated on concepts frequent in web caption pretraining, and performance on genuinely caption-rare concepts collapses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary detectors are evaluated by holding out benchmark classes from detection training, but the held-out class names are typically common words that appear abundantly in web-scale image-text pretraining corpora.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-class zero-shot detection quality is primarily predicted by concept frequency in the caption pretraining distribution rather than by benchmark-defined novelty, so claimed open-set generalization is mostly retrieval of pretrained name-appearance associations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying the novel classes of a standard open-vocabulary detection benchmark by estimated caption-corpus frequency will show a strong monotone relationship with per-class AP, with the rarest stratum performing near a trivial baseline.
why_important: If open-vocabulary detection quality is bounded by caption frequency, deployment claims about detecting arbitrary user-specified concepts are unsupported, and the field needs benchmarks with verified caption-rare classes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Concept-frequency analyses exist for zero-shot classification, but a systematic frequency-stratified audit of open-vocabulary detection benchmarks, and the resulting reinterpretation of novel-class AP, may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate concept frequencies from a public caption corpus, bin the novel classes of a standard open-vocabulary detection benchmark by frequency, and compare per-bin AP across several public open-vocabulary detectors.
main_risk: Concept-frequency estimation is confounded by synonyms and multi-word expressions, and a noisy estimate could smear a real effect or manufacture a spurious one.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Novel-class AP on open-vocabulary benchmarks is broadly read as evidence of generalization to arbitrary unseen concepts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The held-out split controls what the detection head saw, not what the text and vision encoders saw during web pretraining, so the novel classes are novel in name only.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public open-vocabulary detector, rank its novel-class AP against generic word-frequency statistics as a proxy for caption frequency, and check the rank correlation in a single analysis session.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detection AP is a property of the query vocabulary list, not the detector: adding or removing distractor class names materially changes scores and method rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary detectors score regions against a user-supplied list of class name embeddings, so the score of any class depends on which other names are present through normalization and competition effects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reported AP values are unstable under reasonable changes to the query vocabulary, and the size of this instability exceeds typical gaps between competing methods, making vocabulary composition an uncontrolled experimental variable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating several public open-vocabulary detectors under multiple realistic vocabulary variants, such as adding plausible distractor names or removing absent classes, will change absolute AP noticeably and will flip at least some pairwise method orderings.
why_important: If vocabulary composition drives reported differences, open-vocabulary detection leaderboards are not comparing detectors under a fixed measurement protocol, and deployment behavior with user vocabularies is unpredictable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is well known for classification, but a controlled study of vocabulary-composition sensitivity as a leaderboard validity problem for detection may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a benchmark and a set of public open-vocabulary detectors, construct several vocabulary variants of the class list, evaluate all combinations, and quantify within-method variance against between-method gaps.
main_risk: Vocabulary variants must be realistic; adversarially chosen distractors would prove sensitivity but not that ordinary usage suffers from it.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats the benchmark class list as a neutral protocol detail and attributes AP differences to model quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scoring against text embeddings makes the class list part of the model head, and heads with different competition structure are different classifiers even when the backbone is identical.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One detector, one benchmark, three vocabulary variants: measure AP shifts in an afternoon of inference and compare them to published-style method gaps measured on the same setup.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detectors lack a calibrated none-of-the-above: their scores cannot express that a region matches no queried concept, causing systematic false positives when the true object is outside the vocabulary.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text-query detectors assign each candidate region similarity scores to the supplied names, and deployment vocabularies rarely cover everything present in the scene.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When the true category of an object is absent from the query vocabulary, open-vocabulary detectors systematically relabel it as the nearest queried concept with high confidence, rather than suppressing it, and this failure is invisible in standard benchmarks whose vocabularies cover all annotated objects.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing evaluation episodes where some annotated categories are deliberately excluded from the query vocabulary will reveal a high rate of confident nearest-neighbor relabeling errors, and this rate will be much higher than for closed-vocabulary detectors with a background class.
why_important: Real deployments almost never enumerate the full world vocabulary, so nearest-concept relabeling is a central but unmeasured failure mode for open-vocabulary detection.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Out-of-vocabulary behavior of open-vocabulary detectors seems under-evaluated; a dedicated protocol for vocabulary-truncation stress testing may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a standard detection benchmark, evaluate public open-vocabulary detectors with vocabularies that exclude a rotating subset of ground-truth classes, and measure the rate and confidence of predictions that land on excluded objects.
main_risk: Benchmark annotations are incomplete, so some apparent relabeling errors may be legitimate detections of unannotated objects, requiring careful manual auditing of a sample.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] It is assumed that low similarity to all queried names naturally suppresses out-of-vocabulary objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Similarity scores are relative and uncalibrated across queries, and score normalization over the supplied list actively pushes probability mass onto the nearest queried name.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One detector, one benchmark, drop one frequent class from the vocabulary, and count how often its instances are confidently detected as a semantically nearby queried class.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detectors are context classifiers in disguise: pasting objects into atypical scenes collapses their naming accuracy far more than it collapses closed-vocabulary supervised detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web image-caption training pairs objects with their typical scenes, and captions often name objects that are only recognizable from context, so region-text alignment can learn to score regions by context rather than by object appearance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Open-vocabulary detectors rely more heavily on surrounding context for naming than supervised detectors do, so out-of-context objects are misnamed or missed at a disproportionately higher rate.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a cut-and-paste evaluation where objects are composited into atypical scenes, the relative AP drop of open-vocabulary detectors will exceed the relative drop of supervised closed-vocabulary detectors evaluated on the same composites.
why_important: Context dependence undermines the core use case of open-vocabulary detection, finding things where they are not expected, which includes safety-relevant scenarios like hazards in unusual places.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context sensitivity of detectors has been studied for supervised models, but a controlled comparison showing that language-supervised detection amplifies context reliance may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build composites by pasting segmented objects into scenes where they are contextually implausible, evaluate matched pairs of open-vocabulary and supervised detectors, and compare in-context versus out-of-context performance ratios.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts affect models differently, so the study needs artifact controls such as pasting objects into their original scene at a new location.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Web-scale pretraining is assumed to make detectors more robust to unusual configurations, not less.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Caption supervision rewards predicting names from whole-image gist, and region-level alignment inherits this shortcut, whereas box-supervised training forces reliance on in-box evidence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Paste a handful of object categories into a few dozen implausible scenes, run one open-vocabulary and one supervised detector, and compare their out-of-context recall in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Detect-anything claims fail at realistic vocabulary scale: open-vocabulary detection quality degrades systematically as the query vocabulary grows toward thousands of concurrent names.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks evaluate open-vocabulary detectors with vocabularies of at most a few thousand classes, while the advertised use case is detection over an effectively unbounded concept space queried concurrently.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] AP per class declines monotonically and substantially as concurrent vocabulary size increases, because score competition and calibration drift across many names dominate, so performance reported on small vocabularies materially overstates realistic large-vocabulary operation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Holding the evaluated classes fixed and padding the query vocabulary with increasing numbers of valid distractor names will show a clear downward trend in AP for the fixed classes across all tested public detectors.
why_important: The vocabulary-scaling behavior determines whether open-vocabulary detectors can actually replace ensembles of specialized detectors in production systems with large ontologies.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Vocabulary-size scaling of detection quality, as an explicit measured curve with fixed target classes, seems rarely reported despite being cheap to produce.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a set of annotated target classes, evaluate detectors with nested vocabularies of increasing size built from real category names, and plot per-class AP against vocabulary size.
main_risk: Distractor names semantically overlapping the targets would conflate vocabulary-size effects with genuine ambiguity, so distractor sets need semantic distance controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Open-vocabulary detectors are presented as handling arbitrary vocabularies, with vocabulary size treated as operationally neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every added name is an added classifier direction competing for the same regions, and nothing in training calibrates scores across thousands of simultaneous unseen names.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One detector, one benchmark subset, three vocabulary sizes spanning one order of magnitude, and a same-day comparison of AP on the fixed target classes.

one_line_idea: Per-class score incomparability breaks open-vocabulary deployment: a single global confidence threshold is near-meaningless because score distributions differ arbitrarily across queried names.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployed detectors operate at a fixed confidence threshold, and open-vocabulary detectors produce similarity-derived scores whose scale depends on the query embedding, with no training pressure to make scores comparable across names.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The optimal operating threshold varies so widely across queried classes that any single global threshold sacrifices a large fraction of achievable per-class F1, and simple per-class post-hoc calibration on a small labeled sample recovers most of it.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring per-class optimal thresholds on a benchmark will show a wide spread, and per-class thresholding will improve average F1 over the best global threshold by a margin larger than typical differences between competing methods.
why_important: This converts an evaluation abstraction, threshold-free AP, into a concrete deployment defect and offers an extremely cheap fix, per-name calibration, that practitioners currently skip.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Score incomparability is folk knowledge, but quantifying the deployment cost and the recovery from lightweight per-name calibration for open-vocabulary detectors may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public detectors, compute per-class precision-recall curves on a benchmark, compare best-global-threshold F1 against per-class-threshold F1, and measure how much calibration data per class is needed to close the gap.
main_risk: Per-class calibration requires labeled examples per name, which conflicts with the open-vocabulary promise of handling names never seen with labels; the study should also test calibration transfer from related names.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP-based reporting treats thresholding as a detail left to users, implicitly assuming scores are roughly comparable across classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in contrastive region-text training constrains cross-name score scales, and text embedding norms and neighborhood densities vary systematically with name frequency.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One detector, one benchmark, plot the distribution of per-class optimal thresholds and the F1 loss of the best single threshold in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: A scene-prior skyline exposes benchmark weakness: an image-level classifier plus class-agnostic proposals matches open-vocabulary detectors on a large share of benchmark classes without any region-text alignment.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many benchmark categories occur in stereotyped scenes with one or few instances, so image-level presence plus generic objectness can in principle localize them without genuine region-level naming.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A deliberately crude skyline, image-level zero-shot classification for presence combined with class-agnostic proposals and simple heuristics for assignment, achieves a nontrivial fraction of open-vocabulary detection AP, and the classes where it matches full detectors are exactly where benchmarks fail to test region-level grounding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The skyline will be competitive on a meaningful subset of classes, and stratifying benchmark classes by skyline-versus-detector gap will reveal that reported open-vocabulary progress is concentrated on classes the skyline already solves.
why_important: Benchmarks should measure region-level language grounding; if a grounding-free baseline saturates parts of them, those parts measure scene priors and inflate the apparent progress of grounding methods.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Strong trivial baselines are standard practice elsewhere, but a scene-prior skyline analysis for open-vocabulary detection benchmarks appears not to be standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the skyline from public components, evaluate it on a standard open-vocabulary benchmark, and produce a per-class comparison against public detectors.
main_risk: The skyline has design freedom, and a weak implementation would understate the problem; several assignment heuristics should be tried and the best reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Open-vocabulary benchmark AP is read as evidence of region-level language grounding across all classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP rewards any mechanism that ranks correct boxes highly, and for single-instance stereotyped scenes, presence plus objectness is such a mechanism, no grounding required.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Wire together public zero-shot classification and class-agnostic proposal components with a naive assignment rule and evaluate on one benchmark split in a day or two.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detectors cannot certify absence: their scores on object-free images do not support reliable absence decisions, which is the other half of detection that nobody evaluates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many applications need confident absence verdicts, such as confirming that no hazard or contaminant is present, and detection evaluation focuses exclusively on ranked presence quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The distribution of maximum per-image query scores on images lacking the queried object overlaps heavily with scores on images containing it, especially for rare names, so absence decisions from open-vocabulary detectors are much less reliable than presence metrics suggest, and this reliability is uncorrelated with AP across models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring an absence-verification operating characteristic, discrimination between object-present and object-absent images using the maximum detection score, will show weak performance for rare queries across public detectors, and model rankings by absence reliability will differ from rankings by AP.
why_important: Absence certification is a distinct deployment capability with safety relevance, and if it is not predicted by AP, the field's single-number evaluation misses an entire task dimension.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Negative-image evaluation appears in some benchmarks, but treating absence verification as a first-class capability with its own cross-model analysis for open-vocabulary detection may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble verified-absent image sets for a range of queries, compute absence-verification discrimination per query and per model, and correlate with per-query AP.
main_risk: Verifying true absence in source images requires careful annotation, since unannotated presence would corrupt the negative set.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A detector with high AP is implicitly trusted to also indicate absence when it finds nothing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP only constrains the ranking among predictions, not the score scale on empty images, so two detectors with identical AP can differ arbitrarily in absence behavior.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For a handful of queries, collect present and verified-absent image sets, plot maximum-score distributions for one detector, and quantify overlap in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: IoU is the wrong metric below a size threshold: center-distance-based matching reorders small-object detection methods and agrees better with human quality judgments.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] IoU between a predicted and true box is hypersensitive to pixel-level errors when boxes are tiny, and standard evaluation applies IoU thresholds uniformly across scales.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For small objects, IoU-based matching measures pixel jitter rather than useful localization quality, so switching to a scale-appropriate criterion such as normalized center distance changes method rankings and matches human judgments of detection usefulness better.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a pool of detectors on the small-object stratum under IoU matching versus normalized center-distance matching will produce visibly different rankings, and human raters shown matched detections will side with the center-distance ordering more often.
why_important: Metric choice silently steers architecture research; if small-object rankings are IoU artifacts, specialized small-object methods may have been selected for jitter minimization rather than for actually finding objects.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Alternative matching criteria exist in domain-specific literatures, but a direct ranking-stability and human-agreement comparison against IoU for general small-object detection may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-score existing public detector predictions on a benchmark small-object stratum under both criteria, quantify ranking changes, and run a small human study on preference between matched outputs.
main_risk: Center-distance criteria ignore extent errors entirely, which matters for some downstream uses, so the human study must sample diverse use contexts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] IoU thresholds are treated as a scale-neutral gold standard for localization quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same absolute localization error that is negligible for a large object destroys IoU for a tiny one, so uniform IoU thresholds encode an implicit and unexamined scale-dependent strictness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score cached predictions of two detectors under both matching rules on one dataset and check for ranking flips in a single analysis session.

one_line_idea: Sub-pixel translation reveals stride aliasing: small-object detection output oscillates strongly under tiny image shifts because object size interacts with feature stride, a deterministic and fixable artifact.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Convolutional and patch-based backbones process images at coarse feature strides, and small objects span only a few feature cells, so their representation depends on alignment between object position and the sampling grid.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection confidence and even presence of small-object predictions oscillate quasi-periodically as the image is translated by sub-stride amounts, with amplitude growing as object size shrinks relative to stride, making a measurable fraction of small-object misses pure grid-alignment bad luck.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Translating test images in one-pixel steps and tracking per-instance detection scores will show oscillation amplitude inversely related to object size in stride units, and averaging predictions over a few shifts will recover a nontrivial share of missed small objects.
why_important: A deterministic aliasing artifact means part of the small-object gap needs no new learning at all, just anti-aliased inference or architectures, and it also means single-image evaluation of small-object AP has built-in randomness.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift-invariance failures of CNNs are documented for classification, but a quantitative link from stride aliasing to small-object detection misses, with a recovery estimate, may be new for modern detectors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several detectors on shifted copies of a benchmark subset, compute per-instance score variance versus size-to-stride ratio, and measure AP under shift-averaged inference.
main_risk: Border effects and resizing pipelines introduce their own artifacts under translation, so the shifting protocol must crop consistently to isolate grid alignment.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Small-object failure is attributed to insufficient resolution or weak features, with grid alignment treated as negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A one-pixel shift can move a three-cell object across a feature-cell boundary, changing which features see it at all, an effect large models are never trained to smooth out because training crops are randomly aligned.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Shift a few hundred images pixel by pixel through one detector and plot score traces for their small objects within a day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family A-009 (sub-pixel aliasing of prompt-to-mask map); detection stride substrate is distinct.

one_line_idea: Image-level foundation pretraining is a poor donor for small-dense detection: at matched compute, dense-prediction-oriented pretraining beats caption or image-level contrastive pretraining specifically on the small and dense stratum.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Popular vision foundation backbones are pretrained with image-level objectives such as caption alignment, which do not force preservation of fine spatial detail, yet they are widely adopted as detection backbones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The pretraining objective, not backbone capacity, dominates small-object detection transfer, so backbones with dense or region-level pretraining objectives outperform image-level ones on the small-object stratum at equal parameter and compute budgets, even when overall AP looks similar.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A controlled comparison of matched-size backbones with different pretraining objectives, fine-tuned identically for detection, will show the ranking on the small-object stratum diverging from the overall AP ranking, favoring dense-objective pretraining.
why_important: Practitioners select backbones by headline AP and image-level benchmark fame; if the small-object stratum tells a different story, common backbone choices systematically hurt applications dominated by small objects.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Backbone comparisons abound, but an objective-controlled study isolating pretraining-objective effects on the size-stratified detection profile may not exist at matched compute.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune matched-capacity public backbones with distinct pretraining objectives under one detection recipe on one benchmark and report size-stratified AP with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Truly matched compute and data across public checkpoints is hard to guarantee, so conclusions may need in-house pretraining runs at moderate scale to control confounds.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stronger image-level foundation models are assumed to be uniformly better detection backbones across object sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Image-level objectives are optimized by features that discard high-frequency spatial information small objects live in, and fine-tuning may not restore what pretraining never preserved.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare size-stratified AP of two popular matched-size backbones with different pretraining objectives using published detection fine-tunes or one quick fine-tune each.

one_line_idea: NMS makes detection-based counting undercount predictably in dense scenes: there is a characterizable density crossover beyond which suppression errors dominate and density-map methods win.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection pipelines apply non-maximum suppression or learned deduplication, and in densely packed scenes the true boxes of neighboring instances overlap heavily, colliding with the suppression criterion.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image counting error of detection-based counters grows systematically with local instance density and pairwise ground-truth overlap statistics, following a predictable undercount regime, so a scene-statistics measurement can predict in advance whether detection or density-estimation counting will be more accurate.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across scenes binned by local density and mean neighbor IoU, detection-based counts will show monotonically growing undercount bias, with a crossover bin beyond which a density-map approach has lower counting error for the same scenes.
why_important: Practitioners choose counting approaches by convention; a validated scene-statistic decision rule would replace guesswork and would delimit exactly where detection pipelines are trustworthy for inventory, crowd, and biology-style counting workloads.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The detection-versus-density tradeoff is folklore, but an explicit crossover characterization as a function of measurable scene statistics may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take datasets spanning a wide density range, evaluate one strong detector and one density-map method on counting, and model counting error as a function of density and neighbor-overlap statistics.
main_risk: Tuned suppression thresholds partially adapt to density, so the study must sweep suppression settings to show the effect is structural rather than a tuning artifact.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection-based counting is viewed as strictly more informative than density maps and preferable whenever a detector is available.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Suppression decisions are made from box geometry without instance-identity evidence, so beyond a density level the geometry alone cannot distinguish duplicates from neighbors, guaranteeing errors no matter the threshold.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bin one dense dataset by per-image density, plot detector counting bias per bin against a density-map baseline, and look for the crossover in one evaluation session.

one_line_idea: Most claimed small-object method gains are pixel-budget effects: at equal effective input pixels on the object, specialized small-object techniques lose most of their advantage over plain high-resolution inference.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Small-object methods routinely change input scale, tiling, or feature pyramid configuration alongside their core contribution, and inference resolution directly controls how many pixels a small object occupies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When comparisons are controlled for effective pixels-on-object and total inference compute, a large fraction of reported small-object improvements shrinks toward zero, because the operative ingredient was resolution recovery rather than the proposed mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running representative small-object techniques against resolution-matched plain baselines will show the gap on the small-object stratum reducing substantially compared to the originally reported gap.
why_important: If resolution is the dominant lever, the field should optimize resolution scheduling and compute allocation rather than mechanism novelty, and papers need pixel-budget-controlled baselines as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution confounds are acknowledged informally, but a systematic pixel-budget-controlled re-evaluation across multiple published small-object mechanisms may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select several reproducible small-object methods with public code, construct baselines matched on effective object resolution and inference FLOPs, and compare size-stratified AP under the controlled protocol.
main_risk: Exactly matching effective resolution is nontrivial when methods use adaptive or region-dependent scaling, requiring a careful definition of pixels-on-object.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported small-object gains are attributed to the proposed architectural or training mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Input downsampling destroys small-object information before any mechanism can act, so any method that implicitly restores pixels will look good regardless of its stated contribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick one prominent small-object method, run its plain backbone baseline at the resolution that matches its effective pixel budget, and compare small-stratum AP in a day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: prior-art check required: resolution-matched baseline critiques exist for small-object methods; the systematic re-audit is the contribution.

one_line_idea: Tiny-object classification is contextual inference, not appearance recognition: below a resolvable size, detectors name objects from scene context, and context-swap tests expose this hidden dependence.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] At small pixel sizes, the in-box appearance of an object is often insufficient even for humans to classify, yet detectors report confident class labels for such objects on standard benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For objects below an identifiable size threshold, detector class decisions are driven mostly by context rather than in-box evidence, so context manipulation flips tiny-object labels at a much higher rate than large-object labels, and benchmark tiny-object accuracy overstates appearance-based recognition.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Transplanting tiny objects into mismatched contexts, or replacing tiny objects with same-size crops of different categories while keeping context, will flip detector classifications for the tiny stratum at a rate far exceeding the large stratum.
why_important: Applications like distant hazard identification rely on tiny-object labels being evidence-based; if labels are context guesses, confident tiny detections are unreliable exactly when they matter.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context reliance in detection is studied broadly, but a size-resolved quantification isolating the threshold where classification becomes predominantly contextual may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build paired test sets with context-object mismatches at controlled object sizes, run several detectors, and estimate label-flip rate as a function of object pixel size.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts could cue models; controls should include same-category transplants to separate artifact effects from context effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A correct tiny-object label is read as the model having recognized the object from its appearance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When in-box information is physically insufficient, any accuracy above chance must come from context priors, so high tiny-object accuracy is itself evidence of contextual guessing rather than perception.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take a few dozen scenes, swap tiny objects across context categories, and count classification flips for one detector in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Dense-scene errors are dominated by duplicate and merge mistakes that AP barely registers: a dedicated identity-error metric reveals a failure axis invisible in current rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] In crowded scenes detectors produce characteristic errors, one box covering two instances, two boxes on one instance, or systematic miscounts, and AP aggregates these with ordinary misses and false alarms without distinguishing them.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods with similar AP on dense benchmarks differ widely in identity-error rates, merge, split, and duplicate mistakes, and these errors are what downstream tasks like tracking and counting actually suffer from, so an identity-error metric would reorder methods relative to AP for dense-scene use.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Defining and measuring per-scene merge, split, and duplicate error rates on a dense benchmark will show large between-method differences among methods whose AP differs little, and downstream counting error will track the identity metric better than AP.
why_important: If AP is nearly blind to the dominant dense-scene failure axis, dense detection progress is being measured with the wrong instrument, and method selection for crowded applications is misinformed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error-type analyses exist as diagnostic toolkits, but elevating identity errors to a primary reported metric for dense detection, with downstream validation, may be unclaimed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Formalize identity-error definitions on top of ground-truth matching, evaluate a pool of detectors on dense benchmarks, and correlate identity errors versus AP with downstream counting and tracking performance.
main_risk: Identity-error definitions depend on matching conventions in ambiguous crowded ground truth, so the metric needs demonstrated robustness to matching choices.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP on a dense-scene benchmark is treated as a sufficient summary of crowded-scene competence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP is computed from per-box matches and confidences, and a merged box or a duplicate often costs little AP while corrupting instance counts completely.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Implement merge and duplicate counters for cached predictions of three detectors on one dense dataset and compare their identity profiles against their AP in one session.

one_line_idea: Fixed query budgets create a silent recall cliff: query-based detectors fail abruptly when instance count approaches the query count, and the failure is invisible on benchmarks dominated by sparse images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Query-based detection architectures decode a fixed number of object queries per image, and benchmark images mostly contain far fewer instances than the query budget.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Recall of query-based detectors as a function of ground-truth instance count degrades sharply as the count approaches a fraction of the query budget, earlier than the nominal budget suggests, because queries compete and collapse onto duplicate hypotheses, and standard benchmark averages hide this cliff.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Plotting per-image recall against instance count for query-based versus dense-prediction detectors will show a distinctly earlier and steeper decline for query-based models, with the knee position moving as the query budget is varied.
why_important: Dense scenes are the norm in retail, aerial, biological, and crowd domains, so an architecture-level recall cliff determines applicability, and buyers of these architectures deserve a stated instance-capacity curve.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Query-count ablations exist in individual papers, but a cross-architecture instance-capacity analysis framing the effective capacity as well below the nominal budget may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate matched query-based and non-query detectors on datasets spanning instance counts, sweep query budgets for one model, and report recall-versus-count curves.
main_risk: Instance count correlates with object size and image type, so the analysis must stratify or match on these to isolate the count effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The query budget is treated as a generous upper bound with no practical consequence for typical scenes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Queries are trained with one-to-one matching on mostly sparse images, so the learned query distribution allocates effective capacity to typical layouts, not to the combinatorics of packed scenes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public query-based detector, evaluate on the densest available image subset, and plot recall versus instance count in a single evaluation run.

one_line_idea: Benchmark-defined small is not domain small: small-object method rankings established on natural-photo benchmarks invert on scale distributions typical of aerial or microscopy imagery.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The standard small-object definition is an area threshold inherited from natural-photo benchmark statistics, while entire application domains operate at object scales and densities far outside that regime.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Small-object techniques tuned on natural-photo size distributions exploit regime-specific properties, such as context availability and moderate density, so their relative ordering does not transfer to regimes where objects are a few pixels wide and context is homogeneous, and some celebrated techniques underperform simple baselines there.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a fixed pool of small-object methods on natural-photo benchmarks and on genuinely tiny-object regimes will produce rank correlations substantially below 1, with at least one prominent method dropping below a plain baseline in the tiny regime.
why_important: Application engineers import method rankings from mainstream benchmarks; if rankings invert, this common practice actively selects worse methods for the domains that most need small-object detection.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Domain papers note transfer difficulties individually, but a systematic ranking-transfer study across object-scale regimes for small-object methods may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix implementations of several small-object methods, train and evaluate them identically on datasets from distinct scale regimes, and quantify ranking stability across regimes.
main_risk: Cross-domain differences beyond scale, such as modality and annotation style, confound the comparison, arguing for synthetic scale-controlled intermediates as a bridge.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Small-object improvements demonstrated on mainstream benchmarks are assumed to transfer to any small-object application.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mechanisms behind such methods, context aggregation, pyramid fusion tweaks, or scale-aware assignment, each rely on statistics of the training regime that vanish or reverse in extreme-scale domains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two small-object methods with public code and one plain baseline, run them on one genuinely tiny-object dataset, and check whether the mainstream ranking survives.

one_line_idea: Training assignment starves tiny objects: standard positive-sample assignment gives near-zero learning signal to the smallest objects, and oracle-assignment experiments would recover much of the small-object gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector training assigns positives by anchor overlap, center sampling, or matching costs, and all these criteria interact badly with tiny boxes, which overlap few anchors and occupy few feature locations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A disproportionate share of the small-object performance gap originates at training-time assignment rather than at representation or inference, so intervening only on assignment, giving tiny objects guaranteed positives, closes a large fraction of the gap without architectural change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Instrumenting training will show per-instance positive counts collapsing for the smallest stratum, and an assignment-only intervention will improve small-object AP by more than typical architecture-based small-object methods do at equal compute.
why_important: If assignment is the bottleneck, the cheapest fix is a training-rule change rather than new architectures, and many published mechanisms may be indirect assignment fixes that could be replaced by direct ones.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Assignment sensitivity for small objects is known in domain folklore, but a causal attribution study separating assignment from representation via oracle interventions may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log per-instance assignment statistics across sizes during standard training, then retrain with a size-equalized assignment rule and compare size-stratified AP against architecture-based alternatives.
main_risk: Forcing positives onto low-quality tiny-object features could inject label noise into training, so the intervention needs quality-aware weighting variants.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Small-object weakness is mostly framed as a representation-resolution problem requiring architectural remedies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A model cannot learn what it is never supervised on, and if tiny objects receive an order of magnitude fewer positive assignments per instance, the gap could be primarily a supervision-allocation artifact.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Instrument one training run to histogram positive assignments per ground-truth instance by size, a one-day logging exercise that immediately confirms or refutes the starvation premise.

one_line_idea: Size priming in detection: small instances are found mainly when larger same-class instances co-occur in the image, and isolated small objects fail disproportionately, a bias hidden by co-occurrence-heavy benchmarks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark images frequently contain multiple instances of a category at mixed scales, and evaluation aggregates over instances without conditioning on within-image co-occurrence structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors use large same-class instances as within-image evidence that primes detection of small ones, so small-instance recall conditioned on the presence of a larger same-class instance is substantially higher than recall for isolated small instances, and benchmark aggregates mask a much worse isolated-small performance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying small-instance recall by presence versus absence of a larger same-class instance in the image will show a marked gap across detectors, persisting after controlling for scene type and instance size.
why_important: Deployment scenarios such as early detection of a single distant object are exactly the isolated case, so benchmark numbers systematically overstate the capability that matters for early-warning applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Within-image co-occurrence conditioning of recall appears to be an unexplored evaluation axis for size-dependent detection performance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Partition benchmark small instances by same-class scale co-occurrence, compute conditional recalls for several detectors, and verify with paste-based interventions that removing the large instance reduces small-instance recall.
main_risk: Co-occurrence correlates with scene density and context type, so the interventional paste-removal arm is essential to establish causality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-instance detection outcomes are implicitly treated as independent given the image, with recall summaries read as unconditional capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention and context aggregation deliberately share evidence across the image, so a confident large-instance detection can raise feature-level evidence for same-class hypotheses elsewhere, creating the priming dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute the conditional recall split on one benchmark for one detector directly from existing predictions, a pure analysis task requiring no new inference.

one_line_idea: Detectors hallucinate regularity in packed layouts: on grids of repeated identical objects, models fill in missing items at empty positions, revealing pattern-completion behavior in dense detection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Retail shelves, trays, wafers, and agricultural rows present near-periodic arrangements of identical objects, and dense-detection models are trained on many such layouts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors internalize layout periodicity and use it as evidence, so when an item is removed from an otherwise regular grid, models produce confident false positives at the vacated position at rates far above matched non-periodic controls, meaning dense-scene precision partly measures pattern completion rather than perception.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On test sets with items deliberately removed from regular arrangements, false-positive rates at vacated positions will substantially exceed false-positive rates at random empty locations of similar local appearance in non-periodic scenes.
why_important: Counting and inventory systems are deployed precisely on periodic layouts, and a pattern-completion bias inflates counts exactly where users assume detection is easiest, corrupting shrinkage and stock decisions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contextual hallucination is studied for co-occurring different categories, but periodicity-driven same-category hallucination in dense grids may be an unmeasured failure mode.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct removal test sets from real periodic scenes by photographing or compositing gaps, run dense detectors, and compare vacancy false-positive rates against non-periodic controls.
main_risk: Compositing gaps can leave low-level traces; physically photographed removals are the clean version and require modest data collection effort.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense regular scenes are considered the easy case for detection, with errors expected mainly from occlusion and blur.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regular context is extremely predictive during training, and nothing penalizes using it, so a rational learner will absorb layout priors that then override contrary local evidence at vacancies.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph a shelf-like arrangement, remove items, run one detector, and inspect vacancy predictions the same day.

judge_A_meta.anomaly: Pattern-completion in dense detection (confident FPs at vacated grid positions) — perception-vs-prior dissociation with a clean synthetic test.

one_line_idea: Super-resolution preprocessing for small-object detection trades localization gains for classification bias: generative upsampling drags tiny-object labels toward visually typical categories.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative super-resolution is increasingly used to enhance small objects before detection, and generative upsamplers synthesize plausible high-frequency content learned from natural-image statistics rather than recovering true detail.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Super-resolution preprocessing improves box localization for small objects but biases their classification toward categories whose textures the upsampler considers typical, so rare or atypical categories are systematically relabeled as common lookalikes after enhancement, a harm invisible in aggregate AP.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing detection with and without super-resolution preprocessing, stratified by category typicality, will show classification accuracy gains concentrated on typical categories and losses on atypical ones, with confusion flows directed from rare toward common categories.
why_important: Enhancement pipelines are being adopted operationally; a directional labeling bias against rare categories matters for exactly the surveillance and inspection tasks where rare findings are the point.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Super-resolution helpfulness for detection has been evaluated in aggregate, but a category-typicality-resolved harm analysis of generative enhancement may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched detection evaluations with and without a public super-resolution model on small-object data, build per-category confusion comparisons, and test whether label flow is directed toward high-frequency training-typical categories.
main_risk: Effects may depend heavily on the specific upsampler and its training data, so several enhancement models should be tested before claiming generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Super-resolution preprocessing is regarded as a safe, monotone improvement for small-object detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generative upsamplers resolve ambiguity by sampling from a learned prior, and that prior is exactly a typicality bias injected into the evidence the detector then trusts as observation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Enhance a small-object test subset with one public upsampler, run one detector both ways, and inspect the direction of classification flips in a day.

one_line_idea: Long-tail detection gains from reweighting losses are mostly post-hoc calibration in disguise: per-class score recalibration of a plain baseline recovers the bulk of reported rare-class improvements.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail detection methods modify training losses or sampling to boost rare-class AP, and rare-class scores of plain baselines are known to be systematically deflated relative to frequent classes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Much of the rare-class AP improvement from specialized long-tail training reduces to correcting the score scale of rare classes, so applying cheap post-hoc per-class calibration to a vanilla detector reproduces most of the gain without any training change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a standard long-tail benchmark, per-class score transformation of a plain baseline fitted on a small held-out set will close a large share of the gap to representative long-tail training methods, and the residual gap will be concentrated in classes with extremely few training instances.
why_important: If calibration explains most gains, long-tail detection research is re-deriving logit adjustment expensively, and practitioners can get the benefit with a few lines of post-processing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Logit adjustment is established for classification, but a rigorous accounting of how much of detection-specific long-tail method gains is calibration-equivalent may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one plain baseline, fit per-class score calibration on held-out data, and compare against public long-tail methods under identical evaluation, decomposing gains into calibration-explained and residual parts.
main_risk: Detection scores interact with NMS and cross-class ranking, so calibration must be applied before suppression to be a fair equivalent, complicating the pipeline slightly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Long-tail gains are attributed to better rare-class representations learned through modified training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: AP is a ranking metric across images, and deflated rare-class scores lose ranking battles they should win, an error that score transformation fixes without touching the features at all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit a per-class scale-and-shift on a baseline's rare-class scores using a validation split and re-evaluate AP the same day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: adjacent to wave1 calibration cluster (C-002..C-012); the training-gains-are-calibration claim itself is new to the corpus.

one_line_idea: Web pretraining displaces rather than solves the long tail: per-class gains from vision-language pretraining track web caption frequency, leaving web-rare classes as badly off as before.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language pretrained detectors report improved performance on benchmark-rare classes, and benchmark rarity is measured by annotation counts in the detection dataset, not by concept frequency on the web.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The improvement on benchmark-rare classes is concentrated in classes that are rare in the benchmark but common in web captions, so when classes are re-stratified by web frequency, the tail problem reappears essentially unchanged, relocated to web-rare concepts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regressing per-class gains of vision-language-pretrained detectors over supervised baselines on estimated web caption frequency will show a strong positive relationship, and the web-rare stratum will show gains near zero.
why_important: Claims that web-scale pretraining solves long-tail detection guide data strategy; if the tail merely moved, applications with genuinely rare concepts, defects, species, and specialized equipment, gain nothing from the trend.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency analyses of pretraining benefits exist for classification, but a re-stratification of detection long-tail progress by web-concept frequency may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate web caption frequencies for benchmark classes, compute per-class deltas between vision-language and supervised detectors, and compare gain distributions across benchmark-frequency versus web-frequency stratifications.
main_risk: Frequency estimation error and class-name ambiguity could weaken the regression, requiring multiple estimation methods for robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Vision-language pretraining is presented as the practical answer to long-tail detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretraining transfers knowledge proportional to concept exposure, so it can only convert web-common benchmark-rare classes into easy ones while leaving universally rare concepts untouched.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Sort benchmark classes by a quick web-frequency proxy, compare per-class gains of one vision-language detector over one supervised baseline across strata, in a single analysis pass.

one_line_idea: Long-tail methods overfit the benchmark's frequency histogram: retesting under resampled tail shapes reveals that gains are tied to one particular class-frequency profile.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail detection methods introduce hyperparameters and design choices tuned on a benchmark whose class-frequency histogram is one fixed sample of possible real-world imbalance profiles.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gains of published long-tail methods are substantially specific to the tuned frequency profile, so re-creating the benchmark with a different tail shape by subsampling annotations reorders methods and shrinks average gains, revealing profile overfitting rather than general imbalance robustness.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training and evaluating a fixed method pool across several synthetically reshaped frequency profiles of the same underlying data will produce method rankings with low stability across profiles, while a plain baseline plus calibration remains comparatively stable.
why_important: Real deployments face arbitrary and shifting imbalance profiles, so methods that only work on one histogram provide false comfort, and benchmark culture should include profile-robustness as a criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency-profile robustness as an explicit evaluation dimension for long-tail detection methods appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct multiple frequency-reshaped variants of one dataset by annotation subsampling, train representative methods on each, and quantify gain stability and rank stability across variants.
main_risk: Subsampling changes total data volume alongside profile shape, so volume-matched controls are needed to isolate the profile effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A method that improves tail AP on the standard benchmark is assumed to handle class imbalance in general.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many long-tail mechanisms encode the training histogram explicitly or through tuned constants, making them estimators of one distribution rather than robust procedures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Retrain one prominent long-tail method on one reshaped profile of its benchmark and check whether its headline gain over the baseline survives.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-042 (ranking instability under reweighting); training-distribution profile overfitting is the new element.

one_line_idea: Tail classes are recognized by their habitats: rare-class detection succeeds mainly in stereotyped contexts, and out-of-context rare instances fail at much higher rates than out-of-context common ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rare classes have few training instances, which tend to come from a narrow set of scenes, so context and category are more tightly coupled in the tail than in the head of the distribution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors learn tail classes largely as context-conditioned hypotheses, so the context dependence of detection, measured as the performance drop for out-of-context instances, increases systematically as training frequency decreases, making tail AP a measure of habitat recognition.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring per-class context dependence via context-swap composites or context-stratified evaluation will show the dependence anticorrelated with class training frequency across the vocabulary of a long-tail benchmark.
why_important: Rare things in unexpected places are the paradigmatic hard case of open-world perception, and if tail detection is habitat-bound, current long-tail metrics overstate readiness for exactly those cases.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context bias is studied in general, but its quantitative scaling with class frequency across a long-tail vocabulary may be uncharted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build context-swap or context-masking evaluations covering classes across the frequency spectrum, evaluate public long-tail detectors, and fit the relationship between context dependence and training frequency.
main_risk: Constructing fair out-of-context tests for hundreds of classes is laborious, suggesting automation via segmentation-based transplantation with artifact controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Tail-class AP improvements are interpreted as the model having learned the appearance of rare categories.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With few examples, the statistically efficient shortcut is to bind the category to its recurring scene signature rather than to its intrinsic appearance, and training rewards this shortcut.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Transplant a handful of rare-class instances into neutral scenes, run one detector, and compare recall against in-context instances of the same objects.

one_line_idea: Most tail-class failure is naming, not missing: hierarchical evaluation that credits superclass-correct detections reveals the long-tail gap is largely a fine-grained labeling gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard long-tail evaluation scores a detection as wrong when the predicted label differs from the annotated leaf category, even if the prediction is the correct superclass or a sibling category, and tail categories are often fine-grained variants of common concepts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of tail-class errors are detections with correct localization and superclass but wrong leaf label, so hierarchy-aware scoring shrinks the head-tail gap substantially and reorders long-tail methods by revealing which improve perception versus which improve fine-grained naming.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring public long-tail detector predictions with superclass credit will close a substantial fraction of the head-tail AP gap, and the closure fraction will differ across methods enough to change rankings.
why_important: The remedy differs by diagnosis, missing objects call for detection improvements while misnaming calls for fine-grained discrimination or naming interfaces, and current metrics cannot distinguish the two.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hierarchical metrics exist for classification, but a decomposition of the detection long-tail gap into miss versus misname components with method-level consequences may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Map a long-tail vocabulary onto a hierarchy, re-score cached predictions of several methods under leaf-strict and superclass-credit metrics, and compare gap sizes and method orderings.
main_risk: Hierarchy construction choices affect results, so multiple independent hierarchies should be tested for conclusion stability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The head-tail AP gap is read as rare objects going undetected.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness generalizes across related categories, so a detector often finds the rare object but loses the label lottery among fine-grained siblings, a completely different failure than blindness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one method on one benchmark, count how many tail-class misses correspond to overlapping detections labeled with a sibling or parent category, a cached-prediction analysis doable in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Copy-paste augmentation teaches paste detection: rare-class gains from copy-paste partly reflect boundary and compositing cues, and artifact-free insertion tests would show smaller true gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Copy-paste augmentation, inserting segmented objects into new images, is a standard technique for boosting rare-class detection, and compositing leaves low-level traces such as boundary discontinuities and lighting mismatch.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained with copy-paste partially learn to associate the target classes with compositing artifacts, so their measured rare-class improvement is inflated relative to their improvement on naturally photographed rare instances, and the inflation grows with how artifact-prone the augmentation pipeline is.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing rare-class gains on naturally photographed test instances against gains on composited test instances will show systematically larger gains on composited ones, and models will fire more readily on artifact-bearing pasted objects than on seamless insertions of the same objects.
why_important: If augmentation gains are partly artifact recognition, the field overestimates how much synthetic data mixing helps the tail, which distorts data-strategy decisions for rare-category applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositing-artifact learning is discussed for image forensics, but its role in inflating copy-paste detection gains may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without copy-paste, evaluate both on natural rare-class test instances and on composited instances with controlled artifact levels, and compare gain profiles.
main_risk: Building genuinely artifact-minimal composites for the control condition is technically demanding and imperfect controls would blur the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Copy-paste gains are attributed to increased effective sample size for rare categories.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any consistent statistical signature of the augmentation process is a learnable shortcut feature, and pasted-object boundaries are exactly such a signature co-occurring with the boosted labels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one copy-paste-trained public model separately on natural versus pasted rare-class instances and compare its firing behavior in one session.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family B-087 (copy-paste physically invalid for media); artifact-cue inflation for rare classes is the new element; tension with F-005.
judge_A_meta.tension_note: Deliberate tension with F-005 (see F-005 note).

one_line_idea: Repeat-factor sampling helps through contexts, not instances: oversampling images containing rare classes mostly benefits by re-exposing their scene contexts, which context-only controls can demonstrate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Image-level resampling schemes oversample entire images containing rare categories, which simultaneously increases exposure to the rare instances and to their surrounding scenes and co-occurring objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant fraction of the benefit attributed to rare-instance repetition actually comes from re-exposure to rare-class contexts, so a control that oversamples similar contexts without the rare instances, or masks the instances during repeated epochs, retains much of the gain, revealing that the mechanism is context prior sharpening rather than instance learning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training runs comparing standard repeat-factor sampling against instance-masked context oversampling will show the masked variant retaining a nontrivial share of the tail AP gain, contradicting the pure instance-exposure explanation.
why_important: Understanding the causal channel changes what better long-tail training looks like, context synthesis is far cheaper than rare-instance collection, and it also warns that gains may not transfer out of familiar contexts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ablations of resampling schemes exist, but a causal decomposition of resampling benefits into instance versus context channels via masking interventions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched trainings with standard oversampling, instance-masked oversampling, and no oversampling, then compare tail AP and its context-stratified breakdown across the three arms.
main_risk: Masking introduces its own artifacts and removes co-occurrence signal in an unnatural way, so several masking styles should be compared to avoid artifact-driven conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Resampling is believed to work by giving the model more gradient signal on rare-class instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The loss on repeated images is dominated by the many non-rare objects and background patterns in them, so most of the extra gradient actually targets context, not the rare instances.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a trained baseline briefly with instance-masked rare-context oversampling and check for tail AP movement in a short training run.

one_line_idea: Tail-class names are unstable coordinates: rare-category text embeddings shift wildly across synonyms and phrasing, making vision-language long-tail detection fragile in exactly the classes it claims to fix.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language detectors classify via text embeddings, and rare category names occur infrequently in caption corpora, giving the text encoder little evidence to place them stably in embedding space.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of detection performance under synonym and phrasing substitution is much larger for tail classes than head classes, so vision-language long-tail improvements are brittle, and part of measured tail performance is luck in how the canonical benchmark name happens to embed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class AP variance across verified synonym sets will be strongly anticorrelated with class frequency, with tail classes showing swings comparable to their entire claimed improvement over supervised baselines.
why_important: If tail gains depend on name luck, reported long-tail progress from vision-language models is fragile under user vocabulary, and robust naming schemes such as multi-phrase ensembles become necessary components rather than optional tricks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is documented broadly, but its systematic scaling with class frequency in long-tail detection, and the implication for progress claims, may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct verified synonym sets across the frequency spectrum of a long-tail benchmark, evaluate public vision-language detectors under each naming, and regress per-class AP variance on training-name frequency.
main_risk: Rare categories often have few true synonyms, complicating the construction of fair substitution sets for the tail.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A class's zero-shot detection performance is treated as a stable property of the model and the visual category.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Embedding stability comes from training exposure, so the same data scarcity that makes a class rare also makes its coordinate in the classifier space noisy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one detector on ten tail classes and ten head classes under three phrasings each and compare the per-class spreads in one inference session.

one_line_idea: Average tail AP hides intra-tail regression: long-tail methods improve some rare classes while actively degrading others, and worst-group reporting would change which methods look best.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail results are summarized as mean AP over frequency strata, and means cannot distinguish uniform improvement from a mixture of gains and losses across the tail classes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Existing long-tail methods redistribute performance within the tail, improving classes that suit their mechanism while hurting others below baseline, so worst-group and per-class-delta reporting would reveal method profiles that mean-based leaderboards conflate, and would reorder methods for applications caring about all rare classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class delta analysis of public long-tail methods against a shared baseline will show a substantial fraction of tail classes with negative deltas for every method, and rankings under worst-decile tail AP will differ from rankings under mean tail AP.
why_important: Applications with safety-critical rare classes need guarantees on the worst classes, not means, and current reporting invisibly trades some rare classes against others.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Worst-group analysis is standard in robustness literature but appears not to be a norm in long-tail detection reporting.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a baseline and evaluate several long-tail methods per class, publish the per-class delta distributions, and compare mean-based versus worst-group-based method rankings.
main_risk: Per-class estimates in the tail are noisy, interacting with the statistical vacuity problem, so deltas need uncertainty quantification before ranking claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A method with higher mean tail AP is assumed better for rare categories across the board.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mechanisms like margin adjustment or sampling reweighting shift decision boundaries globally, and boundary shifts that help contested classes necessarily hurt their neighbors in feature space.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class deltas of one prominent long-tail method against its own reported baseline from cached predictions and count negatively affected tail classes.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-044 (micro vs macro averaging); intra-tail redistribution and worst-group reporting are the new elements.

one_line_idea: The tail gap decomposes into proposal recall versus classification differently than assumed: for unusual-shaped rare objects the real bottleneck is objectness transfer, not naming, inverting the standard decomposition.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Long-tail detection analyses often assume localization transfers from head classes while classification lags, but tail categories include objects whose scale, aspect ratio, and structure differ strongly from head-class statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The localization-transfers assumption holds only for tail classes that are geometrically typical, and for the subset of tail classes with atypical geometry, thin structures, extreme aspect ratios, or unusual scales, proposal recall is the dominant bottleneck, so the tail is heterogeneous and needs bifurcated treatment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing tail-class errors into proposal-stage misses versus naming failures, stratified by geometric typicality relative to head-class statistics, will show the miss-dominated regime concentrated in geometrically atypical classes.
why_important: A one-size long-tail remedy fails if the tail splits into naming-limited and proposal-limited subpopulations, and detecting geometrically unusual rare objects is common in industrial and scientific applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error decomposition by class frequency exists, but crossing it with geometric typicality to reveal a heterogeneous tail bottleneck may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class proposal recall and naming accuracy for a long-tail benchmark, define geometric typicality from head-class shape statistics, and test the interaction between typicality and bottleneck type.
main_risk: Proposal recall depends on the specific proposal mechanism, so several detector families should be analyzed before claiming generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class-agnostic localization is assumed to generalize to all unseen or rare categories, focusing long-tail research on the classifier.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness priors are learned from the geometry distribution of annotated training objects, and geometry far outside that distribution is exactly where learned proposal mechanisms have never been supervised.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one detector, list tail classes with lowest proposal recall and check by inspection whether they cluster in atypical geometry, an afternoon of analysis on cached proposals.

judge_A_meta.tension_note: Scope-limiter for D-071/D-004: naming dominates except for geometrically atypical classes where proposal recall binds. Kept as the designed counter-claim.

one_line_idea: Boxes already contain masks: frozen features of box-only detectors support high-quality mask prediction with tiny mask supervision, suggesting mask annotation budgets are largely wasted.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Instance segmentation is treated as requiring large mask-annotated datasets, while box annotation is far cheaper, and detectors trained with boxes alone learn rich object-boundary-sensitive features as a byproduct.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information needed for accurate masks is already present in box-trained detector features, so a small mask head trained on a tiny fraction of mask labels atop frozen box-detector features approaches the mask quality of fully mask-supervised models, implying the marginal value of large-scale mask annotation is low.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mask heads trained on progressively smaller mask-label fractions over frozen box-trained features will show a mask-quality curve that saturates early, reaching within a small margin of full supervision at a small percentage of labels.
why_important: Annotation budgets are a first-order cost in applied vision, and if boxes plus few masks suffice, dataset construction strategy across the field should change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weakly supervised instance segmentation exists, but a clean label-efficiency saturation analysis specifically probing what box-only training already encodes may not be established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a box-only detector, freeze it, train mask heads with varying mask-label budgets, and plot mask quality against budget compared to end-to-end mask-supervised baselines.
main_risk: Findings may depend on the detector family and the mask head capacity, requiring a small grid over both to support a general claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] High-quality instance segmentation is assumed to need large-scale mask supervision or a dedicated segmentation foundation model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Precise box regression under scale and occlusion variation already forces features to encode object extent and boundary layout, and the mask head only needs to read this out.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Freeze one public box-trained detector, fit a small mask head on a small mask subset, and evaluate mask quality the same week.

one_line_idea: Segmentation-first detection wins on irregular objects: deriving boxes from class-agnostic masks beats box-first pipelines for thin, curved, and perforated objects, an advantage hidden by benchmark shape statistics.
