judge_A_meta.wave1_note: prior-art check required: learned/appearance-aware NMS exists; the identity-signal-vs-geometry dissociation on dense same-class scenes is the claimed delta.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLM counting is subitizing plus guessing: exact counting holds up to a small integer and then collapses to density-conditioned estimation, a signature invisible in benchmarks that average over count ranges.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal language models are marketed as able to count objects in images, and counting benchmarks typically report a single aggregate accuracy over images whose true counts span a wide range.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model counting behavior decomposes into two regimes, near-exact performance up to a small threshold and coarse magnitude estimation beyond it, with errors in the second regime scaling with the true count and correlating with density cues rather than enumeration, so aggregate benchmark scores mask a qualitative capability boundary.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Count-resolved evaluation will show a sharp accuracy cliff at a small count threshold consistent across models, beyond which error distributions match magnitude-estimation signatures, roughly multiplicative errors, rather than enumeration signatures, occasional off-by-small-integer errors.
why_important: Downstream users treat model counts as enumeration; if large counts are density guesses, applications from inventory to reporting inherit silent multiplicative errors, and benchmark aggregates fail to warn them.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Subitizing-like behavior has been speculated for multimodal models, and a rigorous two-regime characterization with error-signature analysis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build count-controlled image sets spanning exact small counts through large crowds, evaluate several multimodal models, and fit two-regime models to the error structure per model.
main_risk: Confounding between count and visual clutter must be controlled by holding object type and layout statistics fixed across count levels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Counting accuracy is treated as a smooth capability improving with model scale, adequately summarized by one benchmark number.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Exact enumeration requires serial attention-like binding that feedforward vision-language interfaces may not implement, while density estimation is learnable from image statistics, naturally producing the two-regime split.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph controlled arrangements from two to a hundred identical objects, query one model, and plot error against true count in a day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: prior-art check required: VLM subitizing/counting-regime studies exist; the enumeration-vs-estimation error-signature decomposition is the claimed delta.

one_line_idea: Crowding suppresses per-instance recall independent of resolution: detection probability of an instance declines with the number of identical neighbors even when size and image quality are held constant.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense-scene performance is usually explained through small object size and occlusion, and evaluation rarely isolates the effect of instance multiplicity itself at fixed size and visibility.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors exhibit a crowding effect analogous to the one documented in human peripheral vision, per-instance recall falls as identical-instance count rises even with size, spacing, and visibility controlled, driven by suppression machinery and by feature interference among similar neighbors rather than by pixel-level information limits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic and photographed arrays where instance size and visibility are held constant while count varies, per-instance recall will decline measurably with count, and the decline will persist after replacing suppression with oracle deduplication, isolating a feature-level interference component.
why_important: If multiplicity itself degrades detection, dense-scene applications face a previously unquantified error source, and the standard size-and-occlusion explanation of dense-scene difficulty is incomplete.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crowding is a classic perception phenomenon, and a controlled multiplicity-isolated measurement for machine detectors with a suppression-versus-features decomposition may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct count-controlled arrays with fixed instance size and spacing, evaluate several detectors with standard and oracle deduplication, and fit recall as a function of count under each condition.
main_risk: Perfectly controlling visibility and local contrast across counts is delicate, and residual low-level confounds could mimic a multiplicity effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-instance detection difficulty is assumed to depend on the instance's own appearance and visibility, not on how many similar instances share the scene.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both suppression rules and locally pooled features couple nearby similar objects, so the independence assumption is architecturally false and only awaits quantification.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Photograph fixed-size object arrays at several counts, run one detector, and plot per-instance recall against count in a day.

one_line_idea: Counts are cheap detection supervision: adding per-image count labels for classes without box annotations improves detection of those classes, unlocking abundant inventory-style metadata as training signal.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many operational datasets carry per-image counts from inventories, logs, or reports without any box annotation, and detection training pipelines currently have no standard way to consume count-only labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Count labels constrain detector outputs strongly enough, through a differentiable counting consistency loss on predicted detections, to improve AP for count-supervised classes over both box-only baselines and image-level-tag weak supervision, because counts carry instance-multiplicity information that presence tags lack.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mixed-supervision training, boxes for some classes and counts only for others, will improve AP on the count-only classes over tag-only weak supervision at matched data, with the gain increasing for classes that frequently appear in multiples.
why_important: Count metadata already exists at industrial scale for retail, agriculture, and logistics, so validating counts as detection supervision would unlock large training resources at zero annotation cost.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weakly supervised detection from tags is established, and systematic use of exact counts as the weak signal, with an analysis of when counts beat tags, may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate count-only supervision by stripping boxes from selected classes of a standard dataset, train with a counting consistency objective, and compare against tag-supervised and box-supervised references.
main_risk: Counting losses over discrete detections require relaxations whose gradients may be unstable, making the negative result attributable to optimization rather than information content.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Weak supervision for detection is mentally equated with image-level presence tags, with counts not treated as a distinct richer signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A count pins down the exact number of instances the detector must produce, eliminating the degenerate solutions that plague presence-tag supervision, such as firing once on the most salient instance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Strip boxes from three multi-instance classes, train with a simple soft-count penalty, and check for AP movement against a tag-supervised control in a short training cycle.

one_line_idea: Detector-regressor disagreement finds annotation errors: images where detection-based and density-based counts diverge are enriched for ground-truth mistakes, yielding a free annotation-audit signal.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Counting datasets contain annotation errors, missed instances, double marks, and boundary-case judgment calls, and auditing annotations at scale is expensive and unguided.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection-based and density-based counters fail in nearly uncorrelated ways on model-difficult images but agree with each other when the annotation is wrong and the image is easy, so ranking images by paradigm disagreement with the annotation, conditioned on paradigm agreement with each other, concentrates annotation errors far above base rate, enabling targeted re-annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human auditing of images where both paradigms agree with each other but disagree with the label will find annotation-error rates several times the dataset base rate, while images where paradigms disagree with each other will be enriched for genuine visual difficulty instead.
why_important: A cheap, automatic triage signal for annotation quality would improve datasets across counting and detection, and the agreement-conditioned design generalizes to other task pairs with complementary failure modes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Model-disagreement-based label auditing exists for classification, and the cross-paradigm agreement-conditioned variant for counting and detection annotation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run both paradigms on annotated counting datasets, stratify images by the agreement structure among the two models and the label, sample strata for expert re-annotation, and measure error enrichment per stratum.
main_risk: If the two paradigms share failure modes on specific scene types, their agreement stops indicating label error there, weakening the triage in exactly those regions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Annotation auditing is treated as requiring either exhaustive human passes or single-model confidence heuristics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two systems with different inductive biases agreeing against the label is statistical evidence about the label, and the conditioning cleanly separates label suspicion from image difficulty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one public counting dataset, rank images by the agreement-conditioned disagreement score and manually inspect the top fifty for label errors in an afternoon.

judge_A_meta.anomaly: Paradigm-disagreement (detector vs density) conditioned on inter-paradigm agreement as a free annotation-error detector.

one_line_idea: Class-averaged detection AP is driven by a volatile minority: bootstrap analysis shows overall benchmark rankings hinge on a handful of high-variance classes, making leaderboard stability an illusion.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark AP averages per-class AP with equal weights while classes differ enormously in test instance counts, so classes with few instances contribute high-variance terms to the headline number.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of headline AP is concentrated in a small set of low-instance-count classes, method rankings frequently reorder under test-set resampling because of exactly those classes, and reporting AP with class-stratified uncertainty or trimmed aggregation would change which methods appear to lead on established benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Image-level bootstrap of standard benchmark evaluation will show a small class subset accounting for most headline-AP variance, and pairwise method comparisons with small reported gaps will flip in a nontrivial fraction of bootstrap replicates.
why_important: The field's progress narrative is built on small headline-AP deltas, and if those deltas are dominated by a few noisy classes, method selection and research direction are being steered by statistical noise.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Statistical instability of AP has been noted in principle, but a variance-decomposition identifying the volatile-class structure and its effect on leaderboard order may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap evaluation for a pool of public detectors with cached predictions, decompose headline-AP variance by class, and quantify ranking flip rates as a function of reported gap size.
main_risk: Bootstrap over images approximates but does not equal fresh-data variance, so conclusions should be framed as lower bounds on instability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Headline AP differences of a fraction of a point on major benchmarks are routinely treated as real method differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Equal class weighting amplifies the noisiest terms of the average, an elementary variance effect that per-class instance-count disparities make severe.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap two methods with similar reported AP from cached predictions and count ranking flips across replicates in one session.

one_line_idea: AP rewards unusable predictions: methods gain benchmark points from dense low-confidence box floods that no deployment threshold would keep, so operating-point metrics reorder detection leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] AP integrates precision over the full recall range including regions reachable only at very low confidence thresholds, and deployed systems operate at high-precision thresholds where most of those predictions are discarded.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable share of between-method AP differences on standard benchmarks comes from the low-confidence tail that deployment never uses, so ranking methods by fixed-false-positive-rate operating metrics changes their order, and some celebrated methods derive most of their advantage from tail-region behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recomputing method comparisons under operating-point metrics, recall at fixed false positives per image, will show ranking divergence from AP, with the divergence attributable to the sub-threshold score region by decomposition of the precision-recall curves.
why_important: If leaderboard advantages live below deployable thresholds, the community optimizes and publishes improvements users can never realize, a systematic misallocation of research signal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The critique of full-curve integration is old, but a quantified attribution of modern method gaps to the unusable score region may be undone for current detectors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-score public detector pools under a family of operating-point metrics, decompose AP gaps by score region, and identify methods whose advantages concentrate below practical thresholds.
main_risk: The definition of a practical threshold is application-dependent, so a range of operating points must be reported rather than one arbitrary choice.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] AP is treated as a neutral summary whose improvements translate proportionally to deployed performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Integrating over all thresholds weights curve regions by mathematical convention rather than by use, and nothing forces the low-threshold region to correlate with the high-precision region across methods.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For three public methods, compare AP ranking against recall at one false positive per image from cached predictions in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Detection test sets are effectively smaller than they look: image-level and instance-level near-duplicates inflate effective sample size, understating uncertainty and overstating fine-grained method distinctions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large detection test sets were assembled from web sources with limited dedup tooling at collection time, and statistical treatment of evaluation assumes approximately independent test units.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard detection test sets contain enough near-duplicate imagery, repeated scenes, burst frames, recropped versions, that the effective independent sample size is substantially below the nominal count, so all uncertainty estimates are optimistic and some reported method distinctions fall inside the corrected noise floor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Modern embedding-based near-duplicate mining on standard detection test sets will identify a meaningful duplicate fraction, and recomputing evaluation with duplicate-cluster-aware resampling will widen confidence intervals enough to erase some published-scale gaps.
why_important: Every significance claim on these benchmarks inherits the independence assumption, so quantifying its violation recalibrates the evidential weight of a large body of results.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Duplicate analyses exist for classification training sets, and a duplication-aware statistical correction for detection evaluation sets may be unperformed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine near-duplicates on major detection test sets with embedding similarity plus human verification, form duplicate clusters, and re-evaluate method pools with cluster-level bootstrap.
main_risk: Near-duplicate is a threshold-dependent notion, so results must be reported across similarity thresholds with human-validated calibration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test-set size in images is treated as the effective sample size for judging the reliability of benchmark differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-collected imagery is heavy-tailed in scene popularity, and popular scenes recur across sources, making some duplication a statistical certainty rather than a possibility.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run embedding-based duplicate mining on one benchmark test set and manually verify the top few hundred candidate pairs in a day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-023 (semantic-duplicate contamination); within-test-set effective-sample-size claim is distinct.

one_line_idea: The default detection-count cap censors dense scenes: standard evaluation truncates predictions per image at a fixed limit, so performance on the densest images is systematically unmeasured and methods are blind-ranked there.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard evaluation protocols cap the number of scored detections per image, and some benchmark images contain more ground-truth instances than the cap allows predictions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The prediction cap materially censors evaluation on high-instance-count images, methods differing specifically in dense-scene ability receive nearly identical scores because their differences are truncated away, and uncapped or density-scaled evaluation would reorder methods for dense-scene applications.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recomputing evaluation with raised caps will leave sparse-image scores unchanged while measurably changing dense-image scores and their method ordering, demonstrating that the standard protocol cannot see dense-scene differences.
why_important: Users select detectors for crowd, retail, and aerial workloads using benchmark numbers that are provably insensitive to exactly their regime, a concrete and fixable evaluation blind spot.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The cap is documented as a protocol constant, but its censoring effect on dense-scene method comparison may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate public method pools under a sweep of detection caps, stratify by ground-truth instance count, and measure where scores and rankings become cap-sensitive.
main_risk: Raising caps rewards prediction flooding unless paired with operating-point analysis, so the corrected protocol needs joint design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The evaluation cap is regarded as a harmless computational convenience with no effect on scientific conclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On an image whose instance count exceeds the cap, recall above the cap ratio is mathematically unreachable, so the metric is censored by construction and dense-scene ability cannot register.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score two methods on the densest decile of one benchmark with a raised cap and compare against capped scores in one session.

one_line_idea: Greedy confidence-ordered matching biases AP against certain prediction styles: optimal-assignment scoring changes per-method AP unevenly, revealing that part of measured differences is matching-algorithm artifact.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard AP matches predictions to ground truth greedily in confidence order, and greedy matching is not optimal assignment, so the scored match structure depends on confidence ordering even for identical box sets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods whose confidence ranking correlates differently with localization quality are penalized differently by greedy matching, so re-scoring with optimal bipartite assignment shifts per-method AP unevenly, and some between-method gaps shrink or reverse, exposing a matching-rule component inside reported differences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Optimal-assignment re-scoring of cached predictions will change AP by method-dependent amounts, largest for methods with miscalibrated confidence-versus-IoU relationships, and at least some close leaderboard orderings will flip.
why_important: If the matching algorithm contributes to method differences, conclusions about model quality contain an arbitrary protocol component that a better-founded scoring rule would remove.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Matching-rule sensitivity of detection metrics may be folklore among evaluation implementers, but a quantified method-bias analysis appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement optimal-assignment scoring, re-score a public method pool on standard benchmarks, and analyze which prediction-style properties predict per-method score movement.
main_risk: Optimal assignment has its own debatable design freedoms, such as the objective weighting between IoU and confidence, requiring several variants for robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The greedy matching rule is treated as a definitional constant of AP rather than a choice with method-dependent consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Greedy algorithms are order-sensitive by nature, and confidence order is a model output, so the protocol couples scoring to a model property unrelated to detection correctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score two stylistically different methods, one query-based and one dense, under greedy versus optimal matching from cached predictions in a day.

one_line_idea: Unreported inference-time enhancements account for a large share of detection leaderboard deltas: equal-inference-budget re-evaluation collapses many claimed architecture advantages.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection results are reported with heterogeneous and inconsistently disclosed inference-time settings, input resolutions, multi-scale testing, flipping, ensemble-like augmentation, and these settings change scores substantially.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Normalizing a representative slice of claimed method improvements to matched inference compute and identical test-time settings will eliminate or reverse a substantial fraction of the deltas, showing that a nontrivial part of perceived architectural progress is unstandardized inference-time expenditure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under a fixed inference-budget protocol, the distribution of method-over-baseline deltas will shift markedly toward zero relative to originally reported deltas, with some prominent orderings inverting.
why_important: If progress partly reflects inference-budget inflation, the field's architecture narrative is distorted and efficiency-adjusted evaluation should become the reporting standard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compute-matched comparisons are advocated in principle, but a systematic re-evaluation quantifying the test-time-settings share of detection progress may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select reproducible methods spanning several years, re-evaluate all under one fixed inference budget and settings profile, and compare normalized deltas against reported deltas.
main_risk: Some methods are architecturally entangled with specific inference procedures, making a fair common protocol genuinely hard to define for them.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported gains are attributed to modeling contributions, with test-time settings assumed comparable across papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Test-time enhancements are cheap score levers with inconsistent disclosure norms, and any inconsistently applied lever inflates the apparent variance of modeling quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two methods with claimed gaps, equalize resolution and disable test-time augmentation for both, and re-measure the gap in one session.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-045 (hidden budgets); inference-compute axis is distinct.

one_line_idea: Benchmark precision is annotation-limited for top detectors: a substantial share of their scored false positives are correct detections of unannotated objects, so measured precision differences among strong models are annotation artifacts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection ground truth misses instances due to annotator fatigue, ambiguity, and protocol limits, and evaluation charges every unmatched prediction as a false positive regardless of whether the object is really there.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For current strong detectors on standard benchmarks, the fraction of scored false positives that are actually correct detections of unannotated objects is large enough that measured precision saturates against the annotation rather than against model ability, and between-model precision differences at the top of leaderboards mostly reflect differential alignment with annotation habits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human re-auditing of stratified samples of scored false positives from several top detectors will reclassify a substantial fraction as true objects, and correcting the ground truth will compress the precision spread among top models while leaving weaker models comparatively unaffected.
why_important: If top-model comparisons are annotation-noise comparisons, current leaderboard order among strong systems carries little information, and benchmark refresh with model-assisted exhaustive annotation becomes a priority.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Missing-annotation effects are known in principle, and a quantified saturation analysis showing top-of-leaderboard compression under corrected ground truth may be new for current model generations.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample scored false positives across models and confidence strata, obtain multi-annotator verdicts under the original guidelines, rebuild corrected ground truth for the audited subset, and recompute the model comparison.
main_risk: Auditors influenced by model predictions may over-accept plausible boxes, requiring audit designs with prediction-blind verification arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scored false positives are treated as model hallucinations, and precision differences as genuine capability differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: As models surpass the annotation's completeness, the evaluation increasingly measures the annotation, an inevitable crossover that the field has no monitoring mechanism to detect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Audit one hundred high-confidence false positives of one top detector against the original annotation guidelines and report the reclassification rate.

one_line_idea: Annotation conventions drift within datasets: box tightness and part-inclusion practices vary across annotation batches, and detectors learn the average, producing systematic per-batch evaluation bias.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large datasets are annotated over time by changing worker pools under evolving instructions and quality control, and dataset cards do not expose batch-level annotation provenance to users.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Measurable annotation-style drift exists within standard detection datasets, recoverable by clustering annotation geometry statistics, models trained on the full data learn a style average that mismatches every batch, and evaluation error correlates with the batch-style distance from the average, meaning part of measured localization error is style mismatch rather than model imprecision.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Unsupervised analysis of ground-truth geometry, tightness proxies, part-inclusion signatures, will reveal batch-like structure within datasets, and per-cluster evaluation of one model will show localization scores varying by cluster beyond sampling noise.
why_important: Style drift inflates apparent model error, contaminates cross-dataset comparisons, and suggests style-conditioned training or evaluation as a cheap accuracy recovery.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotator disagreement is studied on repeated annotations, and forensic recovery of latent batch-style structure inside standard detection datasets may be unattempted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract geometry-style features from ground truth, cluster annotations, validate cluster reality against any available provenance metadata, and measure model localization error stratified by cluster.
main_risk: Style clusters could confound with scene-type clusters, so scene-controlled analysis is required to isolate annotation style from content.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A dataset's annotations are treated as one consistent convention defined by its published guidelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instructions underdetermine pixel-level decisions, worker pools change, and quality control is sampled, so convention drift is the expected outcome of the production process, not an anomaly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute tightness-proxy distributions over annotation time or file ordering for one dataset and test for non-stationarity in one analysis session.

one_line_idea: Granularity-ambiguous aggregates drive outsized detection error: stacks, piles, and clusters annotated inconsistently as one-or-many account for a disproportionate share of both false positives and misses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real scenes contain aggregations, stacked plates, fruit piles, paper bundles, where the instance decomposition is genuinely ambiguous, and annotation guidelines resolve such cases inconsistently or not at all.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Instances belonging to ambiguous aggregates carry error rates several times the dataset average for strong detectors, the errors are dominated by decomposition mismatch rather than detection failure, and excluding or tolerance-scoring the aggregate stratum meaningfully changes both absolute scores and method rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Flagging aggregate-ambiguous regions on evaluation subsets will show error concentration in that stratum across all models, high between-model agreement in predictions there despite label disagreement, and ranking shifts under aggregate-tolerant scoring.
why_important: If a definitional stratum dominates residual error, model comparison is noise-ranked by aggregate-handling luck, and annotation standards for aggregates would improve benchmark validity more than model changes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Instance-definition ambiguity is acknowledged, and its quantified contribution to detection error budgets with ranking consequences may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate aggregate-ambiguity flags on evaluation samples, compute stratified error budgets for a model pool, and re-score under decomposition-tolerant matching that accepts any consistent instance decomposition.
main_risk: Tolerance scoring for decompositions is technically involved, needing careful definition of acceptable decompositions to avoid rewarding degenerate outputs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Every ground-truth instance is treated as an objectively correct unit that models should reproduce exactly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where one object ends and the next begins in a pile is partly a convention, and charging models for convention mismatches conflates perception failure with definitional disagreement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Flag aggregates in a few hundred images, compute one detector's error rate inside versus outside the flagged regions, and compare in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: High-IoU evaluation operates beyond the human agreement floor: inter-annotator box IoU distributions show that strict-threshold metrics score models against noise, and noise-floor-normalized metrics change conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection metrics include strict IoU thresholds as a precision-of-localization probe, and every ground-truth box is one annotator's draw from a distribution of defensible boxes for that object.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The distribution of inter-annotator IoU varies strongly by object size, boundary clarity, and occlusion, strict-threshold metrics frequently demand agreement beyond the human floor for whole object strata, and normalizing thresholds by the measured local noise floor produces materially different model scores and method orderings in the precision regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Repeated annotation of stratified object samples will show human IoU floors below strict evaluation thresholds for identifiable strata, and noise-normalized re-scoring will compress precision-regime differences among top methods while re-ranking some.
why_important: Scoring beyond the measurement floor manufactures fictitious differences, and a noise-aware metric would realign the localization-precision race with actually measurable quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotator variance for boxes has been measured in pockets, and a stratified noise-floor map integrated into evaluation as threshold normalization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect multi-annotator boxes over stratified samples, estimate stratum-wise IoU floors, define floor-normalized thresholds, and re-score a public model pool comparing conclusions.
main_risk: Multi-annotator collection is costly, and floor estimates depend on annotator quality, requiring expert-versus-crowd calibration arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strict IoU thresholds are treated as objective probes of localization precision, applicable uniformly across objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A metric cannot meaningfully resolve differences finer than the reproducibility of its ground truth, a basic measurement principle that uniform strict thresholds ignore.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Double-annotate a few hundred boxes across size strata and compare the human IoU distribution against the strict thresholds in use.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-025/C-066/B-091 (annotation ceilings); box-geometry noise-floor normalization is the new instrument.

one_line_idea: Detectors out-localize their own training labels: model predictions are systematically closer to multi-annotator consensus than the single-annotator boxes they were trained and evaluated on, so evaluation penalizes models for being right.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training and evaluation use single-annotator boxes, learning theory predicts that models trained on noisy targets regress toward the conditional mean, and the conditional mean of defensible boxes may be more accurate than any single draw.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For well-trained detectors, predicted boxes lie closer to multi-annotator consensus geometry than the original single-annotator ground truth does, so a measurable fraction of scored localization error is actually the label's error, and evaluating against consensus would raise measured model quality and differentially re-rank methods by their denoising ability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On objects with newly collected multi-annotator consensus boxes, strong detectors' predictions will show smaller distance to consensus than the original labels show to consensus, with the effect largest on blurry-boundary and occluded objects.
why_important: The result would invert the usual reading of localization error, part of it indicts the benchmark, and would justify consensus-based evaluation subsets for the precision regime.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-denoising by models is known for classification, and a geometric demonstration that detectors surpass their own box supervision may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect consensus boxes for stratified samples, compute label-to-consensus and prediction-to-consensus distances for several detectors, and test the ordering with occlusion and boundary-clarity stratification.
main_risk: Consensus of several annotators is itself an estimate, and systematic annotator biases shared across annotators would not be exposed by consensus comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ground-truth boxes are treated as strictly more accurate than model outputs, making all deviation model error.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over thousands of noisy examples during training lets the model estimate the annotation distribution's center, which beats any individual sample from that distribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Triple-annotate a hundred objects, compare one detector's boxes and the original labels against the consensus in one annotation-plus-analysis cycle.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-010 (models better than labels); localization-consensus substrate is new.
judge_A_meta.anomaly: Detectors out-localize their own training labels; evaluation penalizes models for being right — measurable with consensus re-annotation.

one_line_idea: Model confusion matrices partially replicate annotator confusion: class-label errors in detection datasets are structured by visual similarity and annotation workflow, and models inherit these exact confusions, inflating measured semantic error.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Class labels in detection datasets contain errors that are systematic, similar-looking categories and interface-adjacent choices get swapped, and evaluation treats the annotated label as truth when scoring model classification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The label-error confusion structure of a dataset, estimable from re-annotation samples, aligns measurably with the confusion structure of models trained on it, beyond what visual similarity alone predicts, so part of measured classification error reflects faithful learning of annotation mistakes, and cleaning training labels would reduce exactly the aligned confusions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Confusion-matrix alignment between annotator errors and model errors will exceed the alignment predicted by an independent visual-similarity model, and label-cleaning interventions on training data will reduce the aligned confusion cells disproportionately on cleanly re-annotated test data.
why_important: Distinguishing inherited-label error from perceptual error changes both the interpretation of benchmark semantic-error rates and the expected return of label-cleaning versus model-improvement investments.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label noise inheritance is studied for classification datasets, and the annotator-model confusion-alignment methodology for detection labels may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate annotation confusion from expert re-annotation samples, estimate model confusions on cleaned test data, fit alignment beyond visual-similarity controls, and run a training-label-cleaning intervention arm.
main_risk: Expert re-annotation defines the reference truth, and expert disagreement on genuinely ambiguous categories limits how sharply annotator error can be estimated.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Model classification errors on benchmarks are read as pure perception failures against a clean reference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models are optimized to reproduce the labeling process, not the world, and any systematic component of the labeling process is signal to the optimizer, indistinguishable from truth.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate the most confused category pairs for one dataset sample and check whether annotation swaps concentrate on the same pairs as model confusions.

one_line_idea: Sparse-annotation training teaches contextual self-censorship: detectors trained under incomplete labeling learn context-dependent suppression of valid detections, producing deployment blind spots that complete-annotation fine-tuning reverses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Several large detection datasets label only a subset of present instances per image by protocol, and training treats unlabeled regions as negatives, penalizing the detector for finding real but unlabeled objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The false-negative supervision of sparse annotation is context-structured, certain categories are systematically under-labeled in certain scene types, so detectors learn scene-conditional suppression rules, detecting an object in one context and suppressing the same appearance in another, and these learned blind spots persist invisibly because evaluation shares the annotation sparsity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On exhaustively re-annotated evaluation subsets, sparse-trained detectors will show context-dependent recall gaps aligned with the training data's under-labeling structure, and brief fine-tuning on completely annotated data will recover recall specifically in the previously suppressed contexts.
why_important: Context-conditional blind spots are the worst kind of deployment failure, systematic, silent, and correlated with scene type, and identifying their annotation-protocol origin gives a concrete remediation path.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Missing-label training effects are studied as uniform noise, and the context-structured suppression hypothesis with its persistence and reversal predictions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Map under-labeling structure of a sparse dataset via exhaustive re-annotation samples, evaluate sparse-trained detectors on complete annotations stratified by that structure, and run the recovery fine-tuning arm.
main_risk: Exhaustive re-annotation at sufficient scale is the main cost, and under-labeling structure estimation needs enough samples per context cell.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Missing labels are treated as diluted supervision that mildly lowers recall uniformly rather than as structured anti-supervision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The optimizer receives consistent negative gradient for specific appearance-context combinations, which is precisely a training signal for conditional suppression, not random noise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Exhaustively annotate a small scene-stratified image sample, evaluate one sparse-trained detector, and look for context-aligned recall gaps in a short annotation sprint.

judge_A_meta.anomaly: Sparse-annotation training teaches context-conditional self-censorship — learned suppression rules invisible to sparse evaluation.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmentation leaderboards measure mask-proposal quality, not language grounding: swapping the text encoder barely moves scores while swapping the class-agnostic mask generator moves them dramatically.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dominant open-vocabulary segmentation systems decompose into a class-agnostic mask proposal stage and a region-text classification stage, and reported gains are usually attributed to better vision-language alignment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Variance in benchmark scores across published systems is dominated by the proposal stage, so cross-system comparisons mostly rank mask generators rather than grounding methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A factorial experiment crossing several proposal networks with several region classifiers will attribute the majority of score variance to the proposal factor, and oracle-proposal experiments will compress the gaps between grounding methods substantially.
why_important: If grounding contributions are small relative to proposal contributions, the field's claimed progress on language grounding is partially an artifact of engineering the segmentation stage, and research effort is being misallocated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle-mask ablations appear in individual papers, but a systematic cross-method variance decomposition separating proposal quality from grounding quality may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a benchmark, cross three public mask proposal models with three public region-text classifiers plus an oracle-mask condition, and run a two-factor analysis of the resulting mIoU matrix.
main_risk: Proposal and classification stages interact (classifiers are tuned to their proposal distribution), so naive component swapping may understate what jointly-trained systems achieve.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community reads open-vocabulary segmentation gains as evidence of better vision-language alignment, treating the mask stage as a solved commodity component.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-agnostic mask quality varies widely across generators and directly upper-bounds every downstream metric, whereas region classification over a fixed vocabulary is comparatively saturated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one published open-vocabulary segmenter, replace its proposals with oracle ground-truth masks and separately with a weaker proposal network, and compare the two deltas to the gap between the top published methods.

one_line_idea: Two-stage segment-then-classify pipelines are structurally biased against stuff categories because cropping a region for classification destroys exactly the context that defines stuff.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Region-based open-vocabulary classification typically feeds cropped or masked regions into an image-level VLM, and stuff categories such as ground, wall, or vegetation derive identity partly from spatial context and extent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The crop-and-classify interface causes a systematic thing-versus-stuff performance asymmetry that is a property of the interface, not of the underlying VLM's knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying open-vocabulary segmentation errors by thing versus stuff will show the two-stage pipelines losing disproportionately on stuff relative to single-stage dense-similarity methods using the same backbone, and context-preserving classification variants will recover a large part of the stuff gap.
why_important: Stuff classes cover most pixels in typical scenes, so an interface-level bias against them caps real-world usefulness of the dominant architecture family regardless of backbone progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Thing-stuff gaps are reported descriptively, but attributing the gap causally to the cropping interface via controlled context-preservation interventions may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark with thing and stuff annotations, compare crop-based, masked-attention-based, and full-image-context region classification over identical proposals and backbones, reporting thing and stuff mIoU separately.
main_risk: Stuff categories also have noisier ground-truth boundaries, so part of any observed gap may reflect annotation ambiguity rather than the classification interface.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Researchers treat region classification as category-neutral and expect scaling the VLM to lift things and stuff equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A cropped patch of grass, carpet, or asphalt is often visually ambiguous in isolation; the VLM never sees the spatial support that disambiguates it, so no amount of backbone scaling fixes the interface.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Classify ground-truth regions from one scene-parsing validation set through the same VLM twice, once as tight crops and once with full-image context and mask pooling, and compare stuff-class accuracy between the two modes.

one_line_idea: Training-free attention-surgery methods for dense CLIP-style inference gain mostly by spatially denoising features, and simple spatial smoothing of unmodified features recovers much of their improvement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A family of training-free methods modifies the final attention block of contrastive VLMs (for example replacing query-key attention with self-self variants) and reports large zero-shot segmentation gains attributed to better localization.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of these gains comes from generic spatial regularization of noisy patch maps rather than from genuinely improved patch-to-text alignment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying plain local smoothing or graph-based label propagation to vanilla patch-text similarity maps will close a large share of the gap to attention-surgery methods, and combining surgery with smoothing will show strongly sub-additive gains.
why_important: Correct attribution matters: if the mechanism is denoising, effort should go into principled spatial priors rather than increasingly exotic attention rewiring, and claimed alignment insights may be overstated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention-surgery papers compare against vanilla baselines but may not control for the trivially available smoothing confound in a systematic mechanism study.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On two zero-shot segmentation benchmarks, evaluate vanilla features, vanilla plus smoothing, attention surgery, and surgery plus smoothing over the same backbone and prompts, and measure gain overlap.
main_risk: Different surgery variants may have genuinely different mechanisms, so a single representative method could over- or under-state the family-wide conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] These modifications are believed to reveal latent dense alignment hidden by an ill-suited final attention pattern, a representational insight rather than a filtering effect.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Self-similarity attention is mathematically close to feature-space non-local smoothing, so the operation may simply be an adaptive denoiser wearing an architectural costume.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one benchmark, four conditions (vanilla, smoothed, surgery, surgery plus smoothed) run in an afternoon; sub-additivity of the last condition is the key readout.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: prior-art check required: training-free dense-CLIP surgery literature discusses smoothing effects; the sub-additivity falsification is the claimed delta.

one_line_idea: Text-to-patch similarity maps in contrastive VLMs localize by visual salience rather than by language: irrelevant text queries still highlight the same salient object.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Patch-text similarity heatmaps are widely used as evidence that contrastive VLMs ground language spatially, and qualitative figures usually show queries for objects that are also the most salient image content.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large component of these heatmaps is query-independent salience, so grounding demonstrations conflate language conditioning with generic foreground detection.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring the correlation between similarity maps for the correct query and for mismatched or nonsense queries will reveal high query-invariance on single-salient-object images, and reported grounding metrics will drop sharply on images with multiple co-salient objects.
why_important: If dense grounding is partly salience masquerading as language understanding, methods built on these maps inherit a failure mode that appears exactly when language conditioning matters most, in multi-object scenes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Salience confounds are acknowledged informally, but a quantitative decomposition of patch-text maps into query-invariant and query-dependent components may not have been carried out.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a set of images, compute similarity maps under correct, wrong-category, and pseudo-word queries; decompose map variance into query-invariant and query-dependent parts; and relate the query-dependent share to grounding accuracy.
main_risk: Softmax normalization choices across queries can artificially inflate or deflate apparent query dependence, so the decomposition must be done on raw similarities with care.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Heatmap figures are read as demonstrating that the text query causally selects the highlighted region.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive training rewards patches that align with any plausible caption content, and captions overwhelmingly describe salient foregrounds, baking a query-independent foreground prior into patch geometry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One afternoon: fifty multi-object images, similarity maps for correct versus swapped queries from one public VLM, and a paired comparison of how often the argmax region even changes when the query changes.

one_line_idea: Class-agnostic mask generators impose a granularity prior that mismatches linguistic category boundaries, capping open-vocabulary segmentation regardless of grounding quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary pipelines rely on class-agnostic proposals whose notion of an object comes from the mask model's training distribution, while text queries can refer to merged regions, parts, or unconventional groupings.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of open-vocabulary segmentation error is granularity mismatch, cases where no available proposal aligns with the linguistically correct region, and this fraction is invariant to improvements in region classification.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Computing the best-achievable IoU over all proposals per ground-truth region will show a substantial oracle gap concentrated in part-like and merged-region categories, and this gap will persist across classifier upgrades.
why_important: It identifies where the pipeline's ceiling actually is: if granularity mismatch dominates, research should target language-conditioned proposal generation rather than better region classification.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle-proposal ceilings are computed occasionally, but decomposing the ceiling by linguistic granularity type and showing its invariance to classifier quality may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a benchmark with diverse category granularities, compute per-category oracle-proposal IoU for a standard proposal set, categorize residual errors into granularity types, and verify the gap is unchanged when swapping in a stronger classifier.
main_risk: Proposal sets can be made enormous by multi-scale sampling, blurring the notion of a fixed granularity prior; the analysis needs a compute-matched proposal budget.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The pipeline view assumes proposals are sufficiently exhaustive and that scaling the VLM classifier is the binding constraint.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask models are trained on datasets with a specific object granularity convention, and nothing in their training encourages producing regions matching arbitrary linguistic construals.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one proposal generator: report oracle-assignment mIoU next to actual mIoU, split by categories judged part-like versus canonical objects, in a single evaluation run.

one_line_idea: Dense language-grounding quality scales with caption richness (words and noun phrases per image) rather than raw pair count, making data curation for dense tasks orthogonal to curation for classification.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] VLM pretraining datasets are curated mainly for image-text semantic match, and scaling studies report image-level metrics; dense alignment is a byproduct with no dedicated curation signal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Holding pair count fixed, pretraining on densely descriptive captions yields markedly better patch-level language alignment than sparsely captioned data, because multi-noun captions force sub-image correspondences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled pretraining runs on caption subsets matched in size but differing in noun-phrase density will produce models whose zero-shot dense segmentation differs substantially while zero-shot classification differs little.
why_important: It would give a concrete, cheap curation lever for dense-capable foundation models and explain why models with similar classification scores diverge widely on segmentation transfer.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-quality scaling work focuses on image-level filtering metrics; caption-density as the controlled variable targeting dense outcomes may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain two medium-scale contrastive models on equal-sized caption subsets stratified by noun-phrase count per caption, then evaluate both on zero-shot classification and zero-shot dense segmentation probes.
main_risk: Caption density correlates with image complexity and source domain, so subsets must be matched on image statistics to isolate the text-side variable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More pairs and better global match quality are assumed to improve all downstream granularities together.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A caption naming five objects provides implicit spatial supervision through compositional co-occurrence that a one-noun caption cannot, and dense alignment is exactly the capability starved by one-noun data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Skip pretraining: stratify an existing model's per-image dense-probing accuracy by the caption density of its nearest pretraining neighbors as a correlational pilot before committing to controlled runs.

one_line_idea: Retrieval-based dense labeling, transferring labels from retrieved segmented neighbors in frozen VLM feature space, can rival learned open-vocabulary segmentation heads while being training-free and instantly extensible.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation methods invest in learned decoders and alignment modules, while frozen VLM features are known to support strong image-level retrieval.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Nearest-neighbor transfer of masks from a labeled support corpus via patch-level correspondence in frozen VLM space recovers most of the accuracy of trained open-vocabulary heads, indicating the heads mostly re-implement retrieval.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A pure retrieve-and-transfer pipeline with a moderately sized support set will reach within a small margin of trained open-vocabulary decoders on standard benchmarks, and its errors will overlap heavily with the trained heads' errors.
why_important: If true, the community's decoder engineering is repackaged nearest-neighbor inference, and the honest baseline for every new method should be retrieval; it also enables instant vocabulary updates without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Retrieval baselines exist for classification and few-shot segmentation, but positioning corpus-scale retrieval as a serious rival to trained open-vocabulary segmentation decoders may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a support index of segmented images embedded by a frozen VLM, label query pixels by correspondence-weighted votes from retrieved neighbors, and benchmark against published trained heads using the same backbone.
main_risk: Support-corpus coverage becomes the hidden variable; a favorable support set could overstate the claim, so coverage must be controlled and reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Learned alignment decoders are assumed to extract dense knowledge that simple non-parametric methods cannot reach.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen features already encode correspondence-quality similarity; decoders trained on limited segmentation data may mostly learn to exploit that same similarity structure with extra steps.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark, implement mask transfer from the top retrieved neighbors of each validation image using off-the-shelf features and compare mIoU to a published training-free and a published trained method.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: prior-art check required: retrieval-based/training-free dense labeling exists; the errors-overlap-with-trained-heads claim is the delta.

one_line_idea: Language-grounded segmenters lean on scene-context correlations so strongly that they segment object regions correctly even when the object itself is erased, revealing context-driven rather than evidence-driven masks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contextual co-occurrence is a known shortcut for image-level recognition, but dense prediction is presumed to be anchored to local pixel evidence since output is per-pixel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Open-vocabulary segmenters produce substantially unchanged masks for a queried object after the object's pixels are inpainted away, in proportion to the class's contextual predictability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On images where queried objects are removed by inpainting, models will still place above-chance mask mass in the original object location, and the effect size will rank classes by contextual predictability rather than by size or frequency.
why_important: Context-driven dense predictions are a safety problem in exactly the applications that motivate open-vocabulary segmentation, such as robotics and inspection, where absence must be detectable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Object-removal probes exist for classifiers and detectors, but a class-stratified quantification for open-vocabulary dense models linking mask persistence to context statistics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct an inpainted-removal set from a segmentation benchmark, query models for the removed class, and measure residual mask mass in the original region versus a matched control region.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts can leak object cues; artifact controls with unrelated-region inpainting of equal area are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-pixel outputs are assumed to be grounded in per-pixel evidence, with context providing only a mild prior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The features feeding dense heads aggregate wide context by construction, and training never penalizes contextual hallucination because queried objects are almost always present in training pairs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inpaint fifty objects out of benchmark images with an off-the-shelf editor, run one open-vocabulary segmenter on the removed class, and report how often the predicted mask still lands on the vacated location.

judge_A_meta.anomaly: Masks persist after the object is inpainted away — the cleanest context-over-evidence falsification in the wave.

one_line_idea: Prompt ensembling, a free win for zero-shot classification, is a mixed blessing for dense prediction: it helps region interiors but systematically blurs boundaries by averaging spatially incompatible similarity maps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Averaging text embeddings over many prompt templates is standard practice inherited from zero-shot classification and is applied unchanged in dense pipelines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Different templates induce systematically different spatial supports for the same class, so embedding averaging trades boundary precision for interior recall in dense tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Boundary-zone metrics will degrade or stagnate under prompt ensembling even as interior and overall IoU improve, and per-template similarity maps will show measurable spatial disagreement concentrated at boundaries.
why_important: Boundary quality drives downstream utility in editing, measurement, and medical applications; an inherited classification trick may be silently taxing exactly that property.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt ensembling effects have been studied for accuracy, but their spatial decomposition into interior versus boundary effects for dense prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate single-template versus ensembled prompts for one dense zero-shot method, reporting interior IoU and boundary F-measure separately, plus inter-template spatial variance maps.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to annotation tolerance settings, so conclusions need robustness checks across tolerance radii.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Prompt ensembling is regarded as strictly beneficial and granularity-neutral, a default hyperparameter rather than a spatial intervention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Each template is a slightly different classifier with its own spatial response profile; averaging classifiers with misaligned decision boundaries in image space necessarily smooths the ensemble's spatial transitions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark, ten templates: compare boundary F-measure of the best single template against the ensemble in one evaluation sweep.

one_line_idea: Fine-tuning VLMs on segmentation data narrows the open vocabulary at pixel level much faster than at image level, so standard image-level forgetting checks certify models that have already lost dense open-vocabulary ability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation systems commonly fine-tune on a closed-vocabulary segmentation dataset and verify retained generality via image-level zero-shot checks or held-out class lists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Vocabulary forgetting is granularity-dependent: pixel-level alignment for unseen classes collapses earlier in fine-tuning than image-level alignment, because dense losses overwrite patch geometry while sparing the pooled embedding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Tracking both image-level zero-shot accuracy and dense zero-shot IoU on unseen classes across fine-tuning checkpoints will show the dense metric collapsing substantially earlier and deeper than the image-level metric.
why_important: The community's standard evidence for retained openness would be shown to be systematically miscalibrated for dense models, affecting how every fine-tuned open-vocabulary segmenter is validated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Catastrophic forgetting is well studied, but a granularity-resolved forgetting analysis contrasting pooled versus patch-level alignment dynamics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a contrastive VLM with a standard segmentation head on a closed class set, checkpoint frequently, and evaluate unseen-class performance at both granularities per checkpoint.
main_risk: The dense and image-level evaluations differ in intrinsic difficulty, so collapse must be measured as relative degradation from the pretrained starting point, not absolute scores.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a fine-tuned model still classifies unseen categories zero-shot at image level, its open-vocabulary segmentation ability is assumed to be similarly intact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense fine-tuning gradients act directly on the spatial feature map with many pixels per image, delivering far more parameter pressure on patch representations than the pooled path ever receives protection for.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public fine-tuned open-vocabulary segmenter and its pretrained backbone, evaluate both at both granularities on the same unseen class list, and compare the two degradation ratios.

one_line_idea: Referring expression segmentation benchmarks are largely solvable by detecting the head noun and picking the most salient instance, so reported scores overstate relational language understanding.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring expression datasets were collected from human games and descriptions, and human speakers systematically refer to salient objects, yet benchmark scores are interpreted as measuring compositional grounding.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A deliberately language-lobotomized baseline that extracts only the head noun and selects the largest or most salient matching instance captures a large fraction of benchmark performance, bounding how much relational understanding scores can actually reflect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The head-noun-plus-salience baseline will achieve a substantial fraction of full-model accuracy on standard referring segmentation benchmarks, and the residual gap will concentrate in the minority of samples with multiple same-category instances.
why_important: It recalibrates the field's progress narrative: architectures credited with relational reasoning may be scoring on samples where reasoning is unnecessary, misdirecting architecture research.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Language-ablation baselines have appeared for older datasets, but a maintained, adversarially strong shortcut baseline reported alongside modern VLM-based referring models seems absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the shortcut baseline with an off-the-shelf detector and saliency ranker, evaluate on standard referring segmentation validation sets, and stratify both the baseline and a state-of-the-art model by same-category distractor count.
main_risk: Defining the head noun robustly requires parsing that itself uses language understanding; the baseline must be kept demonstrably shallow to support the conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark gains are read as improvements in grounding compositional and relational language.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dataset construction never enforced that expressions require relations to disambiguate, and human referring behavior actively minimizes required listener effort, biasing benchmarks toward shortcut-solvable samples.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run an existing open-vocabulary detector on head nouns extracted with an off-the-shelf parser, pick the highest-scoring instance, and score this pipeline on one referring benchmark validation split in a day.

judge_A_meta.wave1_note: wave1 family C-089 (blind-baseline template); referring skyline is a new substrate.

one_line_idea: Referring models fail to ground text-dependent references (objects identified by written labels in the image) even when the same system reads that text correctly in a question-answering mode, revealing an OCR-grounding integration gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Modern multimodal LLMs demonstrate strong scene-text reading, and referring interfaces are being built on them with the assumption that all their capabilities compose.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reading text and grounding masks are served by weakly integrated pathways, so expressions whose disambiguation requires reading in-image text produce near-chance instance selection despite intact reading ability verified separately.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenes with multiple similar objects distinguished only by visible written labels, models that answer questions about the labels correctly will nonetheless select the wrong instance when asked to segment by label, at rates far above their non-text-dependent error rate.
why_important: Text-bearing disambiguation is ubiquitous in retail, industrial, and document-adjacent scenes, and capability composition is the central promise of building dense interfaces on multimodal LLMs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scene-text understanding and referring segmentation are mature separately; a compositional audit isolating their integration for dense outputs may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate scenes with two-plus similar labeled objects, verify per-model reading via targeted questions, then evaluate label-based referring segmentation on the same scenes and compare conditional accuracies.
main_risk: Reading verification and grounding tests must use matched resolution and cropping, since text legibility is resolution-sensitive and could confound the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a multimodal model reads text and segments objects, the community assumes it can segment objects identified by text.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask-decoding heads typically attend to visual embeddings shaped for object semantics, while OCR ability may live in separate token pathways that the mask head never queries.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty scenes with labeled duplicate objects, one segmentation-capable multimodal model, paired reading questions and referring queries, tabulated as a two-by-two of reading success versus grounding success.

one_line_idea: No-target referring, correctly refusing to segment when the expression matches nothing, is the dominant unsolved failure mode: models confidently produce masks for absent referents.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classic referring benchmarks guarantee the referent exists, so refusal is never trained or measured by default, while deployment queries frequently reference absent objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Existing referring models, including those with explicit no-target training, have refusal operating points that collapse under mild domain shift, because absence detection relies on dataset-specific score calibration rather than genuine evidence assessment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models tuned to refuse on one no-target benchmark will show large false-acceptance increases when absent-referent queries are drawn from a different distribution of plausible-but-absent expressions, revealing calibration rather than competence.
why_important: A segmentation assistant that invents referents is worse than useless in safety-relevant workflows; refusal robustness is the gating property for real interactive use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] No-target evaluation exists, but a cross-distribution stress test distinguishing calibrated-threshold refusal from evidence-based refusal may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or take models with refusal ability, construct absent-referent queries via three generation strategies of increasing plausibility, and measure false-acceptance rates across strategies and datasets.
main_risk: Absent-referent plausibility is hard to control; generation strategies need human validation that the referent is genuinely absent yet contextually plausible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adding a no-target class or threshold during training is considered to have addressed the absent-referent problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A learned threshold on matching scores is a distribution-specific patch; nothing forces the model to represent the difference between weak evidence and absence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public no-target-capable model, swap category names in valid expressions to plausible absent categories on the same images, and measure how often a mask is still produced.

one_line_idea: Multi-target and exception referring expressions break single-instance architectural priors: models emit exactly one mask because their decoders structurally assume one referent.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most referring architectures decode a single mask per expression, while natural instructions frequently quantify over sets, as in expressions naming all instances or excluding some.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Set-referring failure is architectural rather than linguistic: models represent the correct set internally (recoverable by probing) but the single-mask decoding interface forces an arbitrary instance choice.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Probes on intermediate representations will decode the full referent set with high accuracy on samples where the final output covers only one instance, and interface-level fixes such as iterative decoding with exclusion will recover most of the gap without retraining the backbone.
why_important: It locates the bottleneck precisely: if set information exists internally, the fix is cheap interface redesign, not new pretraining, changing the field's research agenda for instruction-driven segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-target benchmarks are emerging, but the internal-representation-versus-interface decomposition via probing may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-target expressions, train linear probes on frozen intermediate features to predict per-instance membership, compare probe recall to output recall, and test an iterative mask-then-exclude decoding wrapper.
main_risk: Probe success can overstate usable information if the probe exploits features the decoder cannot access; controls with matched-capacity probes on shuffled labels are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Set-referring failures are attributed to insufficient multi-target training data, implying data collection as the remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The backbone sees rich instance evidence and the language model parses quantifiers competently; only the one-mask bottleneck discards the set structure at the very last step.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Wrap one public single-target model with iterative query rewriting that appends exclusions of already-found instances, and measure multi-target recall gain on a small annotated set.

one_line_idea: Round-trip referring, where a model generates an expression for a region and then must comprehend its own expression, exposes grounding gaps invisible to standard one-way evaluation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring generation and comprehension are usually evaluated as separate tasks with separate metrics, and multimodal LLMs are assumed to possess both coherently.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Round-trip failure, where a model cannot locate the region its own generated expression describes, is common and concentrates on relational and fine-grained expressions, indicating generation and comprehension use inconsistent internal groundings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Round-trip localization accuracy will be substantially below one-way comprehension accuracy on matched regions, and the discrepancy will be largest for expressions containing spatial relations.
why_important: Round-trip consistency is a prerequisite for self-supervised improvement loops and for trustworthy interactive agents; measuring it quantifies whether speaker and listener share one world model.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Speaker-listener cycle training exists in older grounding literature, but a diagnostic round-trip audit of modern segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs may not have been reported.
